title: ÆTHER: Refreshing Sway v2 (natural instruments, produced mix)
story: A fresh, breezy morning: the same six-part journey and steady 6/8 sway Jithesh liked in First Love v7, now as a refreshing track, not a romance.

brief.notes: Jithesh 29 Oct 18:54-18:58: First Love v7 takes 1 and 2 are not romantic but the six-part pattern is really good; keep both as refreshing tracks for a future edit, not locked. Fixes: tumbi, flute etc. used unnaturally; heavy echo destroys the natural sound and originality; DJ-style work and pauses break the natural rhythm. 'Keep it natural, keep it rhythmic.' This keeps v7's six-part map and single steady 6/8 sway (pulse 0.55-0.68 measured on take 2) with a dry live-room sound per music-scoring.md rule 16: no echo, no glitch-chopped veena, no reversed swells, no drop-outs. Prompt mode (music_v2). v2, Jithesh 19:06: the no-echo rule is only for those acoustic instruments (tumbi, flute, violin, veena, santoor etc.), which must keep their natural sound; it is not a rule for the whole track. So v2 keeps the leads dry and natural but lets the bed be produced (warm pad, deep bass, soft kick, light room on the bed only). Still no DJ breaks or pauses in the rhythm.

prompt: THE ACOUSTIC INSTRUMENTS MUST SOUND NATURAL: the bamboo flute, solo violin, tumbi, veena, santoor, mandolin, tabla and dholak are recorded dry and close, played by hand, exactly like themselves: no echo or delay on them, no big reverb tails on them, never chopped, glitched, reversed, stuttered or filtered. The rest of the production can be modern and polished: a warm soft synth pad and strings bed, a deep round bass and a soft kick under the tabla, a glossy clean mix. The rhythm keeps flowing: no DJ-style breaks, no pauses, no drop-outs, no build-and-drop. A bright, refreshing, breezy instrumental in the style of South Indian film music, like a fresh morning breeze through coconut palms, a walk by the river at sunrise: light, happy, playful, uplifting, carefree. Not romantic, not sad, not a festival, not heroic. Raga Kalyani (Yaman), a major scale with a raised fourth, sung-style phrasing with gamakam slides and quick natural ornaments. Instruments: a bamboo flute plays the main melody with a real breath sound; a solo violin answers; a bright tumbi plucks short natural playful riffs, never processed; a santoor plays clean cascades; a mandolin and a fingerpicked acoustic guitar keep a light strum; a plucked veena played naturally; soft strings and a warm modern pad underneath; glass bangles and a little ghungroo for sparkle; tabla and dholak for the rhythm, with a deep round bass and a soft kick. RHYTHM IS THE PRIORITY: from 6 s to the last 3 seconds a clear, steady, flowing 6/8 sway like a boat rocking, about 66 dotted-quarter beats per minute, tabla and dholak in the front, never stopping, never thinning out, never pausing; the same tempo all through, the groove only grows a little fuller part by part. Six parts: 0-6 s: the flute alone plays a rising three-note call (root, major third, fifth) over a soft tanpura, then the tabla starts. 6-18 s: light tabla sway, flute and violin trade short cheerful question-and-answer phrases, the tumbi winks in. 18-32 s: the full sway; the flute sings the main bright melody, the mandolin and guitar strum along, santoor answers. 32-46 s: the tabla swings busier; the violin takes the melody, then flute and violin play it together in harmony. 46-58 s: an interlude: santoor cascades and a quick flute and violin duet with natural Carnatic flourishes, the sway still driving underneath. 58-76 s: the fullest part: dholak joins with joyful fills on the same sway, the tumbi bounces, everyone plays the main melody together, bright and fresh. 76-80 s: the flute plays the opening three-note call once more and resolves home over the last tabla phrase. No echo or delay on the acoustic instruments, no glitch, no reversed swells, no risers, no DJ-style breaks, no EDM drops, no side-chain pumping, no silence anywhere.
